Is that because the user is just telling the AI "solve this" and letting it run with a gigantic theorem instead of prompting it along the way?

I ask because I am deeply involved in using AI to formalize my own project (I am essentially done), and have learned a lot about its behavior and where I am needed to step in with new prompting. One of these areas is I think exactly what you describe, and at least in my work, a long drawn-out theorem rarely works unless the supporting code is already heavily modular (in which case, the theorem is in effect modularized into lemmas even if its given as one block).. so when the AI suggests a longer and longer proof, I usually take it as a red flag that either the AI has drifted from my mathematics (it happens, unfortunately) or that its simply chewing on too much or giving Lean too much at once. Then, just prompting some refactorization suggestions usually helps, and I end up continuing with a heavily modular file structure: It's really nice when that starts to pay off and lemma after lemma are short and compile instantly, or when you need a big "finisher", the AI can give you a long but compartmentalized proof that checks on the first try.

So I guess what I am asking is, are you trying to automate the automation, and get it to use the correct architectural/reduction/simplification ideas instead of having to continually prompt it towards that goal?

EDIT: ok from your paper it looks like thats exactly what you are doing. and I want to thank you personally!! :joy:

I am especially curious how you make the definition between "mathlib acceptable" and "technically correct but not up to these standards." This seems like a very fuzzy area, even with a human making the delineation. I'd love to see the guidelines myself, as my code is 100% AI generated and all I can do is control the prompting to try my best to keep it within good architecture design. I have no idea if the code, all of which compiles, would be a horror-show to a mathlib maintainer, or if they would appreciate the modularity that I have enforced.
@Ian Allen We have some high-level guidelines here: https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/values.html

Hi Oliver,

Yes thank you, I've actually read and re-read through that (and the related documents) a number of times. My difficulty is, I am _completely new_ to this environment. I have extreme difficulty parsing many of the (arguably) subjective statements in those documents into actual code examples. And I am prone to just making outright errors when attempting to do so, without examples.

Case in point: early in my project I was upset about the naming conventions that the AI chose. They seemed purely machine-orientated to me, like real AI dream names or something. And I had read through the mathlib standards, and thought I understood things, and started renaming a lot of lemmas.

Well, then while browsing here, I was in Tao's thread about how to spell asymptotic (fight urge to make wholly inappropriate joke yet again) and I could see that the names they were tossing back and forth were fully in line with what the AI was coming up with. So yeah.. at least for me, I need patterns to look at when talking about this kind of thing.

A specific example is this: 

"### Are things in the right files? [](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/values.html#are-things-in-the-right-files)

Placing definitions, lemmas, and theorems in the right files is important. By keeping Mathlib's import tree wide, we reduce the memory footprint for people importing just a fragment of the library and we decrease wall-clock compile time by enabling easier compile parallelisation. Another reason for correct placement is discoverability: we want to make it easy to guess where a definition or lemma might be."

I really really struggled with this, also because I have a strong desire to align correctly from the beginning, not only for eventually external legibility, but for my own project's sanity. I even asked a number of questions here, but there doesn't seem to be a solid standard. Investigating lean4 formalization papers, I could see quite a number of architectures. In the end, I kind of evolved along with my project and the AI's own methods/understanding of classification, and I have the following:

A core file (probably should migrate a number of lemmas here).

Four "presentations" ie models of the mathematics that are interchangeable (bijections):

semanticModel
diophantineModel
geometricModel
inverseBranchModel (for reverse direction on bijections)

each of those is divided into .Semantics.lean, .Valuations.lean, and .Mappings.lean. All of that feeds into

Bijections

Then I have an Analysis section, which imports all of that and provides the central proof of my theory. This is divided more along the lines of the actual argumentations being made as well as some utitility simplifications, so I work with

Analysis/
core
bridges
affine
operators
divergence
cycles

and eventually get my result in cycles. Is this a correct architecture for mathlib? I honestly have no idea. I just hope some day when I can publish it, that somebody can (and wants to) read it.
sorry honestly didnt mean to hijack this thread, I cant help but respond..

Ian Allen said:

I am especially curious how you make the definition between "mathlib acceptable" and "technically correct but not up to these standards." This seems like a very fuzzy area, even with a human making the delineation. I'd love to see the guidelines myself, as my code is 100% AI generated and all I can do is control the prompting to try my best to keep it within good architecture design. I have no idea if the code, all of which compiles, would be a horror-show to a mathlib maintainer, or if they would appreciate the modularity that I have enforced.

I think it is very hard to give a clear metric for what counts as “mathlib acceptable.” There are guidelines that help with design, but the boundary is still somewhat vague. In our work, I use LLM as a judge to approximate human preferences. My hope is that LLMs can learn some of this taste from human-written Lean code and related discussions in their training data.
Apart from basic software engineering requirements, I think a good API should introduce the right abstractions and restate the problem in a cleaner form. Proof-Refactor is an attempt to abstract common substructures in generated proofs and use them to make the proof simpler and more modular. That said, it still misses many subtle aspects of what makes an abstraction good. This is genuinely a hard problem. It may even be related to the true nature of abstraction in intelligence.

I should also mention that some of these thoughts were shaped by helpful discussions with @Chase Norman , which I really appreciate.

Maybe this also helps: https://github.com/CBirkbeck/mathlib-quality
This guideline might be useful too: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib-phrasebook
So I made that skill for my work and for sphere packing and it's been helpful. But I should say, Claude named the skill and that one should not expect that the code that comes out is mathlib quality

his is genuinely a hard problem. It may even be related to the true nature of abstraction in intelligence.

I wonder if at least some of the "fuzziness" of it will turn out to be more well-defined than expected. Lean is right up against formal linguistics. Maybe the problem isn't as much "matching arbitrary human expectations" as it is "humans speaking truth within a very specific pattern of speech."
If you are looking for a concrete metric, maybe one way is to find an abstraction that compresses the relevant complexity. This paper might be helpful: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.20396.
Thank you Yiming, that's an interesting paper. Putting well defined metrics onto slippery subjects is a fascinating topic and is something that came up repeatedly in my professional career.

Proof-Refactor takes inspiration from Numina-Lean-Agent and uses a modified version of lean-lsp-mcp.
